pages.summary: How the Command Window shows numbers.
body: `short` (the default) shows about 5 significant digits, `long` 15; `shortE` and `longE` always in exponent form, `shortG` and `longG` whichever is shorter; `rat` as ratios; `hex` the bits. `compact` leaves out the blank lines around results and `loose` puts them back. The values themselves are never changed, only how they show.

examples.title: One number, several ways
examples.code:
x = pi*1000;
format long
x
format shortE
x
format rat
0.75
format
x

pages.summary: The Command Window emptied; and two commands kept for programs that use them.
body: `clc` clears the Command Window's text (the variables stay). `more` and `echo` are accepted and do nothing here: the Command Window does not page its output, and programs are not echoed.

examples.title: Cleared, and the variables kept

pages.summary: The Command Window's commands and output copied to a file.
body: `diary` alone turns it on or off; `diary filename` copies to that file (`diary` in the current folder unless named), adding to what is there. Links are written as their text.

examples.title: A session's output kept in a file
examples.code:
diary('session.txt')
disp('first line')
x = 2 + 2
diary off
type session.txt
examples.output:
first line
x =

     4


first line
x =

     4

pages.summary: A short tone, and samples played through the page's sound.
body: `beep` plays a short tone (`beep off` silences it). `sound(y, fs)` plays samples between -1 and 1 at fs samples a second (8192 unless given), one channel as a vector or two as a matrix of two columns; `soundsc` first scales the data to fill that range. The program goes on while it plays.

examples.title: A chord of half a second
examples.intro: Run it in the page to hear it.

pages.summary: The time spent in each function and line of programs.
body: `profile on` starts measuring afresh (`resume` goes on adding), `profile off` stops; `profile viewer` shows each function's calls, total and own time and its slowest lines, and `profile('info')` gives the numbers as a structure. Built-in functions count in the lines that call them; programs run slower while profiled.

examples.title: A function profiled

pages.summary: A function's help, and the functions whose help has a word in it.
body: `help name` shows a function's summary, forms and how it works, or a program file's first block of comments, so that programs carry their own help. `lookfor topic` searches the first line of every function's help (all of it with `-all`).

examples.title: A program with its own help
examples.output:
RINGAREA  The area between two circles of radii r1 and r2.
  a = ringArea(r1, r2) with r2 > r1.

pages.summary: What runs the programs: the interpreter, the computer, and its folders.
body: Programs run in Python in the browser (Pyodide): `computer` is `'PYODIDE'`, `isunix` true (its file system is a Unix one), `ispc`, `ismac`, `isdeployed` and `usejava` false whatever the computer. `version` gives the interpreter's version, `ver` the interpreter and the Python, NumPy and SciPy that run it (with an output, as a struct array, nothing printed). `matlabroot` is the folder of the interpreter's files and `userpath` the home folder of your files.

examples.title: Where the programs run
examples.output:
ans =

    'PYODIDE'

ans =

  1×5 logical array

   0   0   1   0   0

ans = 

  1×4 cell array

    {'PyLAB'}    {'Python'}    {'NumPy'}    {'SciPy'}

pages.summary: Environment variables of the Python process that runs the programs.
body: `setenv(name, value)` sets one, `getenv(name)` reads it ('' when it is not set).

examples.title: Set and read back

pages.summary: A web address opened in a new tab; and a program stopped.
body: `web(url)` opens the address in a new browser tab. `exit` and `quit` stop the running program; the page itself closes with its tab.

examples.title: A program that stops on a bad input
examples.intro: The function stops everything when given a negative number; called with 3 it carries on.

pages.summary: Breakpoints set and cleared by command, the breakpoints listed, and the functions running.
body: `dbstop in file at line` makes a program stop before that line with the `K>>` prompt, where variables can be looked at; `dbstop if error` stops where an error is raised. `dbclear` takes breakpoints away and `dbstatus` lists them (the Editor shows them in its margin). `dbstack` lists the functions running, the innermost first, each with its line.

examples.title: None set yet
examples.intro: Breakpoints belong to the page's debugger, so they are set in the Command Window (see the notes below); here the list is empty.
examples.code:
s = dbstatus;
isempty(s)

examples.title: Who called whom

notes: A session: with a function file `twice.m` holding `y = 2*x;` on line 2, `dbstop in twice at 2` and then `twice(3)` stop before that line at `K>>`, where `x` can be shown or changed; `dbcont` runs on, `dbquit` stops, and `dbclear all` takes the breakpoint away.

pages.summary: What the code checker finds in program files.
body: Syntax errors, and in functions: values assigned but never used, inputs never used, outputs never set, results not ended by a semicolon, and a function named unlike its file. Each message has its line and columns; with an output, a struct array with `message`, `line` and `column`.

examples.title: A function with two faults
examples.output:
L 1 (C 25-30): Input argument 'unused' might be unused.
L 2 (C 1-5): The value assigned to variable 'total' might be unused.
L 3 (C 1-3): Terminate statement with semicolon to suppress output (in functions).

pages.summary: Text to and from the system's clipboard.
body: Data that is not text is copied as `mat2str` writes it. In the page the browser may ask whether it may read the clipboard.

examples.title: A matrix copied as text
examples.code:
clipboard('copy', [1 2; 3 4]);
clipboard('paste')

pages.summary: A function that keeps its results for inputs it has had.
body: `memoize(fh)` gives a memoized function: called again with the same inputs, it gives the kept result instead of computing. The last 10 results are kept (`CacheSize`); `Enabled` turns it off. `stats` tells how the kept results were used, `clearCache` forgets one function's, `clearAllMemoizedCaches` every one's.
syntax: A memoized function, called as `y = mf(x)`.

examples.title: The second call kept
examples.output:
ans = 

  struct with fields:

      TotalHits: 1
    TotalMisses: 2
           Size: 2

ans =

     0

pages.summary: The typical time a function takes, in seconds.
body: The function takes no inputs (`@() myfun(x)`); it is run once to warm up and then several times, and the median is given, which is steadier than one timing with `tic` and `toc`.

examples.title: A time in seconds
examples.intro: Times depend on the computer, so the example shows only that it is a short positive time; run it to see the number.

pages.summary: Preferences kept from one session to the next, in groups.
body: `setpref(group, pref, value)` keeps a value (in the home folder); `getpref` reads it, or with a default sets it when it is not there yet; `ispref` tells whether a group or preference is there; `addpref` adds one (an error if it is there) and `rmpref` removes a preference or a whole group.

examples.title: A setting kept, read, and removed
examples.output:
ans =

     2

ans =

    'blue'

ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   0

pages.summary: Indexing and assignment written out as a list of steps.
body: `substruct('()', {2}, '.', 'f')` describes `A(2).f`: a struct array of steps, each with a `type` (`'()'`, `'{}'` or `'.'`) and `subs` (a cell of indices, or a name). `subsref(A, S)` indexes by them and `subsasgn(A, S, B)` assigns, giving the changed A: indexing chosen at run time, and what a class's own indexing receives.

examples.title: A(2).f read and set

pages.summary: A struct's fields as name-value pairs.
body: `{name1, value1, name2, value2, ...}` from a scalar struct, to pass options on: `f(x, C{:})`.

examples.title: Options passed on
examples.code:
opts = struct('LineWidth', 2, 'Color', 'r');
C = namedargs2cell(opts)

pages.summary: Whether the language release, or a toolbox, is older than a given one: always false here.
body: PyLAB follows the language as it is now, so programs that test for an old release take their paths for current ones.

examples.title: A program choosing its path
examples.code:
if isMATLABReleaseOlderThan("R2020a")
    disp('the old way')
else
    disp('the current way')
end
verLessThan('matlab', '9.0')
